https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cg49.text: Image source, Linda Mancuso Image caption, Long Island mother-of-two Linda Mancuso's disabled son Michael, 23, lost a Haitian aide his mother considers a "lifeline" By Sheila Flynn Senior US Reporter Published 1 hour ago Long Island mother-of-two Linda Mancuso has been "praying on a daily basis" that her disabled son's Haitian caregiver will be able to come back to work. It was "horrifying," she says, when Jean, who had a temporary work permit, was laid off from work at the end of July from his position at a nonprofit supporting individuals with developmental and intellectual disabilities. Her son Michael is a 5ft 10in, nonverbal 23-year-old. "Showering, sleeping, eating, tying his shoes - Michael can't tie his shoes - I mean, there's so much hands-on involvement, and Jean did all of that," she says. Mancuso was a ball of nerves when she finally agreed to send Michael to residential care, at the age of 19, calling it "the hardest thing I've ever had to do". When he met Jean in the adult home, however, she felt a sense of peace. "Certain people just have it," she says of Jean. "He's literally a lifeline." But Michael lost that lifeline weeks ago, when his employer had to lay Jean off along with 18 other Haitians. Their temporary protected status (TPS) - which allows eligible foreign nationals from unsafe countries to work in the US - had expired. The Trump administration first announced in June 2025 that it would be removing the TPS for Haitians, and the ensuing legal battle went all the way to the Supreme Court. But America's top judges ruled in favour of the administration, paving the way for 350,000 Haitians to lose their status at the end of July. The stripping of that status meant that holders can no longer legally work in the US and are at risk of deportation. The healthcare industry, with a robust Haitian workforce, has been hit particularly hard - with legions of employers forced to fire TPS holders who work directly with patients. Trump cancelled TPS amid a wave of measures restricting immigration, a central plank of his successful 2024 election campaign. Immigration was one of the top concerns for voters in that election and, in Long Island, both counties decisively backed Trump. More than a dozen countries have had their TPS terminated in Trump's second term and Haitians make up nearly a third of all TPS recipients affected. Families face separation as Haiti TPS scheme ends How US guns flow to gang-ravaged Haiti The care industry is feeling the effects. Haiti numbers among the top five countries from which immigrants in the direct-care workforce come, says Kezia Scales, vice-president of policy and research at the Paraprofessional Healthcare Institute. The industry was already under-staffed and waitlists for many care services - from home health aides to assisted living - were already long. "We simply do not have enough people in our domestic market, when you exclude immigrants, to fill those jobs," she tells BBC News. National advocacy groups are campaigning for policies that would strengthen the long-term workforce - including ones that "would expand legal pathways for international caregivers". When asked about the impact of TPS termination, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told the BBC that "Temporary Protected Status is exactly that - temporary". "The assertion that the only way we can support the healthcare industry is by allowing unvetted illegal aliens to remain in the country is grossly false and lazy," the spokesperson said. Image source, Reuters Image caption, An activist waves a Haitian flag in New York during an August march in support of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians At AHRC Nassau, which employed Jean, CEO Stanfort Perry sounds exasperated and exhausted. The organisation let go of 19 Haitian staff this year and 22 last year, amidst other immigration crackdowns, he says. "It takes us months to recruit one individual to work in this field, train them and prepare them to provide compassionate, caring support to a person with an intellectual and developmental disability," he says. "I'm competing with fast-food restaurants, grocery stores and retail for staff, because they pay more than what we are able to pay," he adds. Image source, Linda Mancuso Image caption, Michael, second from left, is 5'10, 200-plus pounds and nonverbal, needing 24/7 care It's an issue across the country. At Jewish Community Services of South Florida, which lost 18 Haitian TPS holders, the remaining aides are also working overtime. "That is a huge financial strain on a nonprofit like us," says Sarah Katzenstein, the organisation's director of strategic communications and marketing. The loss of TPS caregivers has been especially damaging to seniors served by the Jewish organisation, as many of them are Holocaust survivors, says Katzenstein. "They had relationships with these home care aides for years - some of them for decades," she says, adding that Holocaust survivors especially can have difficulty trusting strangers. "It's a very intimate relationship, so to these clients, the loss of having their Haiti TPS-holding caregivers truly is devastating." Jewish Community Services has been writing to elected officials to advocate for proposed Senate Bill 4814, which would match a bipartisan bill already passed in the House to extend TPS for Haitians. The effort has currently stalled in the Senate, blocked by Republican opposition. Hundreds of Haitians have been deported since the Supreme Court ruling, despite widespread gang violence in the country. White House czar Tom Homan defended the deportations in a recent CNN interview. "The judges made a decision they must go home. And they need to go home... we're just enforcing the law. And we're doing it in a way that the American people voted for." According to polling released last month by AP-NORC , external , support for Trump's overall immigration policy has fallen 10% since the start of his second term but remains relatively strong compared with other issues like the economy. On deportations, about half of US adults surveyed said Trump had gone too far, which is about the same number as the start of the year. A Pew Research survey in June 2025 , external , before the TPS provision was withdrawn from Haitians, suggested 39% of Americans supported the ending of TPS but 59% disapproved. Back on Long Island, Mancuso is grieving the loss of a carer who had actually managed to connect with her high-needs son. "That's one of the things that, as a parent, you worry [about]. Does this kid know that there are other people in the world, other than me, that love him? "And I think he sensed that from Jean - that it's not just a job." Her son might not be able to say it, but she knows he misses Jean and doesn't understand why he's no longer there. For Mancuso, her already-high anxiety about her son's well-being is skyrocketing. "With Jean, I had not a care in the world," she says. She's worried not just for her son but also for the other families served by the local non-profit - and, of course, for Jean and TPS holders like him who are living with uncertainty, unsure if or when they will be deported. "I'm hoping against hope that this thing gets resolved," she says. "I care about [Jean] as a human being, he needs a livelihood - and this has been a livelihood for him, and he's good at it, helping my son. "And it's directly impacting my son by his lack of presence here - and I want him back." Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPA Ukraine Allies did not warn Kyiv of Russian ballistic missile strikes, says Zelenskyy Ukrainian president’s comments on ‘particularly vile’ strikes come after US threatened to halt intelligence sharing Luke Harding , and Andrew Roth in Kyiv Tue 13 Oct 2026 17.54 EDT First published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 09.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukraine received no early warning from its partners about a second night of Russian ballistic missile strikes on civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, including a critical power plant struck after dark, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday. The Ukrainian president had earlier described an attack involving five missiles on Monday as “particularly vile”. He emphasised that receiving intelligence from Ukraine’s western allies “helps saves lives, and this is one of the most critical issues”. “This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he wrote on social media . He did not apportion blame for the lack of warning, calling it unfortunate. More ballistic missiles were then launched at Kyiv on Tuesday night, striking a key power plant in the capital despite a purported energy ceasefire claimed by Donald Trump . One person also died in a strike on a high-rise apartment building, according to the mayor, Vitali Klitschko, who said apartments were on fire and being evacuated. A further 13 injuries were reported. “Once again, ‌no advance warning from our partners. The main target was energy infrastructure, specifically thermal plant No 4,” Zelenskyy wrote on the social media app Telegram, again without explaining why he thought there had been no warning. US officials made explicit threats over the weekend to their Ukrainian counterparts that the Trump administration was on the brink of halting intelligence sharing with Kyiv. On Tuesday, however, Trump denied intelligence sharing had stopped. He told reporters: “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we’re working with them and Russia on getting the war to end.” Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries and has blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in fuel prices in the US. On Friday the US president announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia, dropping previous US sanctions. Read more Asked on Tuesday whether Russia could use proceeds ​from the ​sale to purchase ​more bombs, Trump sidestepped the question. “That’s ​a diesel ‌deal, not ​for ​us. That’s being released into the world. That’s not being released to us,” he said. Earlier the president claimed Moscow and Kyiv had agreed an “energy ceasefire”, something Zelenskyy described as “news to me” . Ukraine’s leader said his military had not struck Russian oil refineries or energy facilities in the two days following Trump’s Sunday announcement. The Kremlin, however, had ignored the “ceasefire” and continued to bomb Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as before, with multiple attacks, he said. “Russia did not heed the president … the Russians sent absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes,” he noted on Tuesday. Ukrainian commanders say American intelligence is not needed to identify targets for deep strikes on Russia, with oil refineries marked on Google Maps. But they say it plays a crucial role in warning of Russian ballistic missile launches, and the takeoff of long-range bomber aircraft. “It is deeply unfair that they are destroying our energy infrastructure while Ukraine receives no warnings about ballistic missile launches,” Zelenskyy said in a statement after the Tuesday strikes. “It is vital that the world does not remain silent about this. And it is crucial that America clearly sees what is happening and who is responsible for the continuation of the war.” The blasts could be heard in central Kyiv as Ukraine’s air defences failed to stop the high-speed Russian missile targeting the capital. The missile strikes on Ukraine’s left bank targeted a thermal power plant, Zelenskyy said, and also struck an apartment building leaving both dead and injured in the latest strike on the capital. Zelenskyy warned on Tuesday evening that Russia was planning further strikes with ballistic missiles, telling Ukrainians: “Please take care of yourselves tonight and tomorrow.” In recent months Russia has dramatically stepped up its bombardment of Ukrainian towns and cities. It has particularly stepped up its attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, cutting power and water in large parts of Ukraine’s capital as emergency workers race to restore basic utilities. Ukraine, meanwhile, has struggled to shoot down incoming missiles and jet-powered drones and has appealed to partners to boost its dwindling supplies of US-made Patriot missiles. According to the Financial Times , the Trump administration has also threatened to suspend the procurement scheme under which Ukraine’s European allies buy advanced US systems, which are then sent to Kyiv, including badly needed Patriots. The Kremlin’s systematic campaign against Ukraine’s power grid has led to widespread blackouts in Kyiv and other cities. Putin’s apparent goal is to shut off heating and electricity for millions of civilians this winter, and to trigger a new wave of refugees into neighbouring EU states. Speaking in Warsaw, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, indicated that cooperation with the US was continuing and said the lack of warning about the Kyiv attack was due to a “special type” of Russian weaponry. On Monday, Russia also bombarded the city of Kharkiv, destroying a residential building. Sharing footage from the scene, Zelenskyy said four people had been killed and 41 injured. Rescuers spent the entire night searching for people trapped under the rubble, he added. Meanwhile, 11 sailors were missing after their ship was sunk by a drone attack off the coast of Bulgaria. The incident prompted Bulgaria to summon Russia’s ⁠ambassador. Two cargo ships were hit ⁠by drones overnight and one ​was sunk, Bulgarian officials said. Bulgaria stopped short of explicitly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks but the prime minister, Rumen Radev, said their outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”. The row between Washington and Kyiv is the most serious since last year, when Trump threw Zelenskyy out of the White House. Ukraine’s president has said he is willing to stop hitting Russian oil refineries – but only on a reciprocal basis and with “real guarantees” that Moscow will cease its attacks on Ukraine’s own energy sites. “Direct or indirect support for Russia, delaying aid to Ukraine and complicating protection of lives from ballistics – this is what will definitely not work for peace. A strong America, a strong Europe , strong partners are needed,” he said on Tuesday.
